title: SheetJS (xlsx) is installed from a vendor download address instead of the npm registry
A hand-written lexical HTML nesting scanner protects the turndown converter from deeply nested pages
Buffers from the sherpa-onnx native binding are copied to satisfy the Electron memory cage

reason: The kit is a Node API that loads a LibreOffice engine into the host process. The Go design keeps the four operations (PDF, format conversion, recalculation, page images) behind an office engine seam and runs the engine as a located child process: by the owner's decision of 2026-11-18 it is the LibreOffice the operator installed, run headless, so the office tools work only where LibreOffice is installed.

sharp binds the native libvips library to check, orient, scale and re-encode attached images. The Go attachment store does the same with the standard library image packages and golang.org/x/image, with limits read from the header before any pixel is allocated; transparent images are stored as PNG because the chosen packages have no lossy WebP encoder.

turndown converts fetched HTML to Markdown for the web_fetch tool. The Go tool uses the html-to-markdown module on the golang.org/x/net/html parser with the same fixed style, plus harness rules that remove hidden content and neutralise table spans.

The plugin adds GitHub-flavoured tables and strikethrough to turndown. The chosen Go module provides both as its table and strikethrough plugins; the upstream replacement rules that ignore colspan become a pass that deletes span attributes before the table plugin runs.

The binding carries ONNX Runtime and runs SenseVoice speech recognition in a managed Node subprocess. The Go provider runs a recognition program the operator installed (the documented example is the prebuilt sherpa-onnx runtime) as a supervised child process, so the host links no inference library; the harness downloads neither a runtime nor a model (DH-ADR-XCUA-4).

ExcelJS parses .xlsx workbooks in a browser Worker for the spreadsheet preview. Under DH-ADR-3 the host reads the workbook with the excelize module and renders an HTML table, so no workbook parser runs in the browser.

SheetJS parses legacy binary .xls workbooks in the browser. The Go design has no BIFF parser: a .xls file is converted to .xlsx by the Office engine and then previewed through the same host reader, which needs the engine to be installed.

PapaParse splits CSV and TSV text into literal string fields for the spreadsheet preview, and rewrites a file list in one build script. The host does the same with encoding/csv from the standard library, with small harness code to keep blank lines and to reject invalid UTF-16.

PDF.js draws PDF pages with selectable text in the browser, parsing in a Worker. The Go design keeps it: the prebuilt pdf.js files are vendored at a pinned version, embedded in the binary and loaded by one small JavaScript island, with the same hardened options and no network fetch.

The client uses it for three small reads of .xlsx parts: theme colours, relationship files and a scan for content the preview cannot draw. In the host these are token walks with encoding/xml from the standard library, which matches names by namespace and resolves no external entities.

The account page compares and rounds decimal balance strings exactly in the browser. The host renders that page, so the comparison and the round-down-to-two-places formatting are done with math/big.Rat from the standard library.

The package is the data model and canvas drawing code of a React spreadsheet editor that upstream uses read-only. The Go interface has no React runtime and renders the spreadsheet preview as an HTML table from the host, so no grid model or canvas code is needed.

The package is the React Workbook component and its style sheet. A server-rendered table with sticky headings, native scrolling and tab requests replaces it; keeping it would need React and a bundler inside an island, against DH-ADR-3.

The patch escapes copied cell values, hides canvas freeze lines and fixes read-only trackpad scrolling in a third-party grid. The Go design has no grid widget: cell text is escaped by the host template engine, and a table has sticky rows and native scrolling, so nothing remains to patch.

The patch stops a render loop on sheet switching, writes formula text as text instead of markup, keeps the selection of each sheet and fixes tab scroll buttons in the React component. With a server-rendered table a sheet switch is a fragment request and formula text is escaped by the template engine, so the causes are gone.

The 35 KB patch makes ExcelJS find parts through relationships, match XML names by namespace, decode UTF-16 parts, keep CDATA and plain-text comments, and fail on missing worksheets. The causes are properties of ExcelJS: the Go reader uses excelize and encoding/xml, which resolve relationships and namespaces natively; the cases not established from source are a requirement with its own test, and no patched dependency is carried.

The entry exempts this kit package from the pnpm minimum release age rule because the kit and its engines are qualified and released together. The Go harness installs no kit package: the office engine is located on the machine and run as a child process, so there is no package age rule to exempt.

The dependency is fetched from one vendor host outside the package registry, so its integrity and availability depend on that host. The Go design drops the legacy .xls parser and converts such files with the Office engine, so nothing is fetched from that address.

Upstream scans HTML by hand to refuse deep nesting because its bundled parser becomes very slow. The Go HTML parser stops with an error when its open-element stack passes 512, so the scanner is not written and the tool maps the error to the same omission text.

The copy exists only because the native binding is loaded into a Node runtime hosted by Electron, whose memory cage forbids JavaScript views onto native memory. The Go design loads no binding into a JavaScript runtime; recognition runs in a separate native process.

Orientation, metadata removal, 16-bit reduction, byte-identical pass-through and first-frame GIF
Scaling rules, the quality ladder, smallest-kept and re-decode verification

Golden Markdown for the fixed style, unchanged text bodies and concurrent use

CSV and TSV grammar, literal fields, blank rows, strict quotes, encodings and the early cell limit
Theme colours, undisplayed-content detection, inert XML parsing and package-bound relationship targets

The rendered table contains hostile strings only as text, has no editing control and a tab request returns one sheet
